headline: Ooor is a 1.5MB local LLM manager that turns llama.cpp into a complete desktop AI workstation
summary: This open-source Windows desktop app integrates llama.cpp engine management, a GGUF model library, and an agent tool-calling layer, all in a tiny 1.5MB executable with no Electron or cloud services.
details: Ooor is a new MIT-licensed, open-source Windows desktop application that weighs just 1.5MB. It transforms the llama.cpp command-line ecosystem into a "click-and-run" local AI workstation.

Built with plain WinForms and .NET Framework 4.8, Ooor avoids Electron and cloud dependencies, launching instantly and idling in single-digit megabytes of RAM. It offers a purely local, private experience with no telemetry or accounts.

The app serves four key roles: a llama.cpp engine manager, a GGUF model library, a Hugging Face model marketplace, and a streaming chat console with an Agent tool-calling layer. It talks directly to llama-server.exe via a local HTTP API.

Its Agent capabilities are a standout feature, supporting the Model Context Protocol (MCP). This allows local models to fetch web content, read/write local files, and analyze data, creating a fully offline research assistant.

Ooor also includes a spreadsheet-like GGUF model manager with soft-delete options, built-in chat with inference speed metrics, and "Profiles" to save engine, model, and agent bindings. It supports English and Simplified Chinese.

Installation is a simple double-click, requiring no admin privileges for daily use. Users can quickly download models from the integrated marketplace, start the llama-server, and begin interacting with their local LLMs.

headline_marked: [[Vogue sent robots down the runway]] at Vogue World, and people were not impressed
headline: Vogue sent robots down the runway at Vogue World, and people were not impressed
summary: Humanoid robots from Unitree performed at Vogue World Milan, an event marketed as a tribute to "the human touch." Their appearance sparked widespread online discussion and mixed reactions from attendees.
details: Vogue World Milan featured humanoid robots from Chinese firm Unitree during "The Age of Intelligence" act. They danced and waved, but were notably not wearing clothes, sparking immediate online reaction.

The event, meant to celebrate Italian craftsmanship and "the human touch," saw a viral moment with Valentino creative director Alessandro Michele's pained expression. This contrasted sharply with the show's stated theme.

The robots overshadowed the fashion itself, becoming the main talking point, much like similar robots at London Fashion Week. This highlights a growing trend of integrating advanced robotics into high-profile cultural events.

Vogue's increasing alignment with tech, evidenced by sponsors like Meta Glasses and OpenAI, and the upcoming San Francisco edition, suggests a strategic pivot. This move aims to leverage tech's financial power and influence.

The appearance of the robots sparked debate about the rapid adoption of technology and the growing wealth of tech titans amidst a cost-of-living crisis. Critics saw it as a symbol of disconnect and concerns over AI, surveillance, and labor displacement.

Some observers, including a tech founder, expressed annoyance at celebrities cheering, viewing it as insensitive given job losses linked to automation. Others felt the robots didn't represent the true innovation in creative technology.
Fashion industry insiders questioned the relevance and visual value of the robots on the runway. While Vogue seeks new revenue streams by partnering with tech, the execution felt "unnatural" to many.
